topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Census and Diversity

data.title: Religious Diversity in Modern Britain
data.sourcePassage: Britain today is one of the most religiously diverse societies in the world. Walk through any major city and you will find churches, mosques, synagogues, mandirs, gurdwaras, and Buddhist centres. Religious communities from around the world have made Britain their home, and this has shaped British culture, food, festivals, and public life. The 2021 census for England and Wales showed a significant change in religious identity compared to previous decades. Christianity remained the largest religion, with 46.2% of people identifying as Christian — but this was a sharp decline from 71.7% in 2001. For the first time, less than half the population identified as Christian. Over a third (37.2%) identified as having no religion. Islam was the largest non-Christian religion at 6.5%, followed by Hinduism (1.7%), Sikhism (0.9%), Judaism (0.5%), and Buddhism (0.5%). Census data must be interpreted carefully. Not everyone who identifies as Christian is a regular churchgoer — many tick 'Christian' because of background, baptism, or cultural identity. Similarly, 'no religion' does not always mean atheism; some people in this category believe in something spiritual but do not identify with an organised faith. Religious diversity is also unevenly spread: it is concentrated in urban areas such as London, Birmingham, Bradford, and Leicester. Rural Britain tends to be more homogeneously Christian or non-religious. Britain's religious landscape is complex and changing — and it requires respectful understanding from all sides.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Religion in Public Life

data.title: Religion in Public Life
data.sourcePassage: Religion plays a significant role in British public life — though this is contested and changing. Britain has an established church: the Church of England, whose Supreme Governor is the monarch. Bishops of the Church of England sit in the House of Lords. Parliament opens with Christian prayer. Bank holidays include Good Friday and Christmas Day. The coronation ceremony is deeply rooted in Christian tradition. At the same time, the state does not enforce religious observance, and freedom of religion or belief is protected by law. Religious organisations are among Britain's most important contributors to social welfare. Food banks — many run by churches, mosques, gurdwaras, and other faith organisations — provide millions of meals each year. The Trussell Trust, the largest food bank network in Britain, has Christian roots. Sikh gurdwaras provided langar (free food) to communities during floods, COVID-19, and other emergencies. CAFOD, Islamic Relief, and Jewish Care provide domestic and international charitable services. Chaplaincy — religious and pastoral support in hospitals, schools, prisons, and the military — is provided to people of all faiths and none. Religious Education (RE) is compulsory in state schools. Its content includes both religious and non-religious worldviews, including Humanism. Faith schools (Church of England, Catholic, Jewish, Muslim, and Sikh) educate a significant proportion of British children and are sometimes controversial. Some argue that faith schools promote divisive identities; others argue they provide excellent education rooted in clear values and community.

topics: Religion in Modern Britain: Interfaith Work and Challenges

data.title: Interfaith Work and Living Together
data.sourcePassage: In a diverse society, how people of different faiths — and no faith — live together is one of the most important social questions. Interfaith work involves people from different religious traditions working together on shared concerns: running food banks, responding to community crises, reducing prejudice, and building mutual understanding. Local interfaith forums bring religious leaders together to discuss community issues and coordinate responses. Schools organise visits to different places of worship and invite speakers from different faiths. Shared projects — from environmental action to anti-poverty work — allow different communities to work alongside each other, building trust through shared purpose. This matters because misunderstanding is a significant driver of prejudice. When people do not know anyone from a different background, it is easy to believe stereotypes. When they work together, stereotypes are harder to sustain. Britain's diverse society also faces real challenges. Islamophobia — prejudice and hostility towards Muslims — has contributed to a rise in hate crimes. Antisemitism — prejudice against Jewish people — has also increased. Media representation sometimes reinforces harmful stereotypes: reporting crimes by individuals of one faith in ways that imply the fault lies with the religion rather than the individual. A critical distinction is essential: religion, ethnicity, culture, and nationality are not the same thing. Not all South Asians are Muslim, Hindu, or Sikh. Not all Arabs are Muslim. A British person can be of any religion or none. Conflating religious and ethnic identities is a form of stereotyping. People of all faiths and none can contribute to community cohesion — the building of a society where different groups respect and trust each other.
